evidence: De La Soul has said they submitted full sample information for '3 Feet High and Rising' (1989), and that Tommy Boy chose which of those samples to clear and which to leave uncleared, including a Turtles sample the label did not clear. The Turtles' Howard Kaylan and Mark Volman sued for copyright infringement in 1991 and the case was settled out of court, reportedly for a large sum. Critics and biographers widely read the group's next album, 'De La Soul Is Dead' (1991), as a direct, more guarded and cynical response to that year, though no single interview ties every change in tone to the lawsuit specifically, which is why this sits at consensus rather than documented.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: The debut is bright, generous with its samples and happy to be liked. Its follow-up opens by smashing the daisy-and-flower image of the first record and turns markedly more cynical throughout, released the same year the Turtles settlement became public.

explanation: Tommy Boy released '3 Feet High and Rising' with an uncleared sample of the Turtles' 'You Showed Me'. The decision about clearing samples was the label's, not the artists': De La Soul say they handed in full details of every sample and Tommy Boy decided what to clear. The Turtles sued in 1991, one of hip-hop's landmark sampling cases, and it was settled. That same year De La Soul released 'De La Soul Is Dead', a noticeably darker, more cynical record that took aim at their own cheerful image. Reading that change as caused by the lawsuit is a critics' consensus rather than a confirmed link, which is why this is held at consensus, on the same rule that a label's decision has to change the artist's music (A69, A121).
